items.originalTitle: Denis Villeneuve on Drastic Changes in His Dune: Part 3 Movie: ‘When You Adapt, You Kill’
items.author: Eliana Dockterman
items.title: Denis Villeneuve on Drastic Changes in His Dune: Part 3 Movie: ‘When You Adapt, You Kill’
items.summary: Timothée Chalamet with director Denis Villeneuve on the set of Dune: Part Three —Courtesy of Warner Bros. Denis Villeneuve is finally done wandering the desert. The writer-director has spent nearly a decade adapting Frank Herbert’s Dune and Dune Messiah, the saga of Paul Atreides ( Timothée Chalamet ), a young duke stranded on the desert planet of Arrakis, the only source of the universe’s most precious commodity, spice. Embraced as a messiah by the native Fremen thanks to the machinations of a religious order called the Bene Gesserit, Paul ends Dune: Part Two by avenging his father, seizing the throne, and launching a war. At the beginning of Dune: Part Three, which opens Dec. 18, billions have died in his name, and Paul faces a conspiracy that includes his wife, Princess Irulan ( Florence Pugh ), and Chani ( Zendaya ), the estranged Fremen mother of his children. The director of previous hits including Sicario, Arrival, and Blade Runner 2049 spoke with TIME about radical adaptation choices in his trilogy’s final chapter and his plans for his next project, a James Bond film, whose new star, Robert Pattinson, was announced a week after our conversation. Fans of Dune Messiah have called the book unadaptable . The book is a chamber piece. People are meeting in rooms talking. It’s a complex, paranoid book. It’s also a kind of depressing book that was not welcomed by Dune readers. The first book is more like an elegy of a hero. And Herbert felt that he was missing the mark because he wanted to create a warning against messianic figures. He felt he needed to correct the trajectory of the story. So yes, it was a big challenge to make this adaptation. The opening battle, which is about 15 minutes in the movie, is one sentence in the book. It’s such a free adaptation that I felt it would have been dishonest to call the movie Dune Messiah. That’s why it’s called Dune: Part Three. The biggest departure is Paul’s love interest, Chani. In the books, she stays loyal to him even after he marries the emperor’s daughter and becomes this messianic figure. In your movie, Paul and Chani have children together, but she later fights against Paul’s regime. Why the change? It all started with the adaptation for Dune: Part Two. I was facing the challenge of trying to embrace Herbert’s idea to create a story that would be a warning, not a celebration. At the end of the first book, Paul wins the battle, marries a princess, still gets Chani, and becomes emperor. When you read the book, you’re like, this is a celebration of a hero. I had the idea to make Chani more of a critic regarding the idea of religious colonization. It’s not in the book, the idea that the older generations are contaminated by the beliefs of the Bene Gesserit, by the colonialist religious poison. And the new generation doesn’t believe in the messiah. They want Fremen to be freed by the Fremen themselves. I thought it was a dynamic idea, Chani being the representation of this. In the third movie, Chani is still a critic of the choices Paul has made. She believes the Fremen should free themselves. She doesn’t want to harm Paul, but she does want to harm his regime. I would have loved to have taken Frank Herbert for a coffee about these ideas because I think he could have liked them. In his book, Chani is there to give Paul foot massages. It’s a character that has not a lot of firepower. Chalamet and Zendaya in Dune: Part Three —Courtesy of Warner Bros. Did you worry about upsetting book purists? When you adapt, you kill. It is not the book. It is my movie inspired by the book, with tremendous respect. My three movies embrace the Bene Gesserit angle because that is what I thought was most inspiring, relevant, and cinematic. But you could make an entire Dune adaptation focused on the idea that humans have fought AI and banned machines. Those ideas aren’t in my movies because it’s too much. You have to make choices. That’s the beauty of adaptation. There is a big time jump between Part Two and Part Three. Paul and Chani have teenage children now. You originally planned to take a long break between those films. What changed? I did [ Part One and Part Two ] back to back, without a single day break between. They were not easy births. I’m not complaining. I’m just explaining that I said to myself while filming Part Two, the only way to get out of this alive is to take a break. I’m going to the forest to hide for many months. And I did. The problem is that after two weeks, I got bored. My wife asked me, “What are you doing?” And I said, “I’m writing Part Three. ” I was waking up at night with cinematic images. I was working on another project, but every image coming to my mind was from Dune Messiah. —David Jon Photography What images? The final one of Paul. It’s a moment that haunted me all these years, and I think I did the trilogy to make that image. One that has stuck with me from the movie is the opening battle. Was there a particular cinematic touchpoint? It’s difficult to see men coming out of a troop transport being decimated without thinking of Saving Private Ryan. It’s obvious. I knew I was stepping into delicate territory because that is one of the most celebrated cinematic sequences of the past 30 years. But I felt it was what the scene needed. I have been dreaming about shooting a landing on the beaches of Normandy since I was a kid. Another was Florence Pugh, covered in clay, walking through the maze to Paul. I don’t believe that was in the book. Where did that come from? At the beginning of Part Three, Paul is unable to find a peaceful way out of the violence. He becomes more and more paranoid and isolated. We’re not sure if he’s lost contact with reality. How do you express that? Princess Irulan has to meet her own husband she hasn’t seen in years. How does he live? How can he protect himself from the assassination attempts? We created a space as if Irulan is walking into the subconscious space of Paul, like the Greek story of Theseus and the Minotaur, where Theseus walks into the labyrinth in order to kill the monster. Irulan won’t kill Paul, but this idea of her going into that maze to neutralize the source of evil was inspiring. You’ve called this your most personal film in a long time. How so? One of the ideas is what kind of world Paul and Chani are trying to leave their children. And what happens to this heritage when you are going through a divorce? That’s a question that anyone who has a broken family understands. It’s vivid and profound to me. Dune: Part Three premieres the same weekend as Avengers: Doomsday. How are you feeling about that? Listen, I will be honest. The first Dune came out at the end of the pandemic. We made a great box office in a very rough environment. But we had the winds against us. Then the second movie, same thing. We were meant to release in the fall, and we had to release at the end of winter because of the two Hollywood strikes. We had success, but it was not easy. The third time, I said to myself, “Finally, there is no pandemic, no strike in sight. We will have a normal release.” Then Disney put the biggest franchise of all time against us. I’m no fool. Those movies are a mammoth. So I was deeply disappointed. But we had committed to this date, to IMAX. It was impossible to move. So I accepted my fate, praying to the gods of cinema. Dune is not a mammoth like the Avengers, but it’s a sexy little animal that has a lot of firepower, and I hope we will survive. It could be one of the biggest box-office weekends of all time because of both movies. Am I in competition with the Avengers ? Absolutely not. It’s a T. rex. But I stand proud because I think the film delivers. After living within Dune for so long, how difficult is it to transition to a different world for James Bond? I don’t sleep a lot right now because it’s like I have electricity in my veins thinking about this new project. It is so different. I spent 10 years of my life in the sun talking about a specific color palette, thinking about ways to embrace natural light. I adore being on Arrakis, but I think it’s healthy to step away. Robert Pattinson in Dune: Part Three —Courtesy of Warner Bros. Are there things you feel are essential to Bond that need to be maintained? I don’t want to talk too much about Bond because it’s still in the oven cooking. This stage of the process is my favorite part because everything is possible. I will say: I love traditions. I love the unapologetic way the character behaves, the panache. I’m not here to change the DNA of James Bond. I’m here to embrace it, to bring it to the world of today. I’m a hardcore James Bond fan, and I want other fans to have fun watching my film. Of course, it will be tainted by my sensibility. But I wake up every morning with a stupid smile because it’s a world of pure cinematic pleasure. We are speaking ahead of the much-anticipated casting announcement. Are you aware that people were placing bets on Polymarket? I read nothing about that. My responsibility is to make the best casting and create the best story for that cast. I cannot listen to the rumors. No matter what we do, we will never please everybody. When Daniel Craig was cast, it was a sh-tstorm. He was blond. He was short. He was not seen as an action hero. Yet when we talk about James Bond today it is because of Daniel Craig’s extraordinary interpretation. And that was a different environment in 2006 before social media. I expect a hurricane when we bring our choice to the world. Some people will be happy. Some will be mad. I can do nothing about that. At the end of the day, the truth will be on the screen. Then they will be able to judge.

items.originalTitle: Cenk Uygur goes all in on Ro Khanna for 2028
items.author: Will Steakin
items.title: Cenk Uygur goes all in on Ro Khanna for 2028
items.summary: Ro Khanna hasn't launched a 2028 bid yet, but he already has a pioneer of the populist left in his corner. Progressive firebrand Cenk Uygur is set to formally endorse the California Democrat on Thursday night during his annual appearance on nephew Hasan Piker's Twitch stream, a Thanksgiving Day debate-a-thon the pair call "Cenksgiving." Uygur told POLITICO he will pitch Khanna as the best populist progressive candidate. His Rebellion PAC will also debut its first 2028 ad promoting a Khanna candidacy Thursday night. "For me, it's a no-brainer," Uygur said in an interview, explaining why he’s backing Khanna. "Who else would you back, and why would any progressive or any populist back anyone else?" Along with his PAC getting behind Khanna, Uygur is also launching his own "Draft Ro" website to collect signatures and showcase other early high-profile endorsers, though he wouldn't say who just yet. The endorsement is one of the first of the 2028 cycle, and it comes before any major candidate has formally announced. Inside Washington, Khanna’s chances are viewed as quite slim. But for Uygur, that kind of underestimation is exactly part of the draw. "I love it," Uygur said of the skepticism. "I wouldn't have backed him if anyone in D.C. was behind him." "We're running against Washington," he added. "So if Washington doesn't like a candidate, perfect." Uygur is pairing his endorsement with a litmus test he’s trying to lay down for 2028 progressives: Candidates must call what Israel has done in Gaza a genocide and support ending U.S. funding for Israel. "It isn't actually about Israel," Uygur said. "It's about: Is this person going to represent us or not?" Khanna, he said, is "among the very, very few, and maybe the only candidate, that'll pass that test." He allowed for one other: "There's also AOC. If she runs, that's another person that could pass the test." But that's as far as the praise goes. His endorsement of Khanna comes as many other progressives are waiting to see whether Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) jumps in. Uygur isn't one of them. Asked if her entry would change his calculus, he said: "Not 1%." "Sorry, but I don't think AOC means it," he said. "I don't think she would do any of the things that she says, and so I'm not going to back someone who is not going to deliver." "She's obsessed with the establishment, so she's going to run a soft, weak race," he added. "She wants to make Democratic leaders and mainstream media happy. Good luck with that strategy." Khanna has told POLITICO he plans to decide whether to run after the holidays and that whether Ocasio-Cortez gets in won't factor into his decision. Uygur's backing could give the potential 2028 candidate some credibility on the populist left, not to mention a boost from "The Young Turks," one of the longest-running and most popular progressive shows online, which Uygur launched in 2002. He also co-founded Justice Democrats in 2017 and ran a long-shot bid of his own for the 2024 Democratic presidential nomination. His Rebellion PAC sparked controversy during the 2026 midterms with an ad tying U.S. funding for Israel to higher grocery prices, which the campaign of then-Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed distanced itself from. Uygur, who was also a prominent backer of Vermont independent Sen. Bernie Sanders' presidential runs, has a blunt prediction for 2028: "I'm positive Ro Khanna is going to win."

items.summary: The MasterChef judge on artichokes, ambition and Irish food It’s an amazing moment when Anna Haugh lets me peel and chop a butternut squash, right there in the kitchen next to her, while she makes a beetroot pickle. The 46-year-old is a fiendish perfectionist and a fierce champion of every last ingredient. She’s making a dish that reflects the sensibility of her restaurant, Myrtle , named after the giant, dynastic wellspring of the Irish food scene, Myrtle Allen . It’s polenta with squash two ways – crushed and pureed – with pickle and goat’s cheese. Every ingredient has a story, and every story reaches back into an epic food tradition. There’s a lot going on, though you really have to see it to know just how much; so although I have the potential to really mess things up, here she has no choice but to let me peel and chop. items.originalTitle: How to Have a More Sustainable Black Friday, According to Experts
items.author: Simmone Shah
items.title: How to Have a More Sustainable Black Friday, According to Experts
items.summary: Black Friday signage displayed in a retail window on Oxford Street on Nov. 23, 2026 in London, England. —Alishia Abodunde—Getty Images Black Friday is here—holding the promise of good deals and the unofficial start of the holiday shopping season. But if you plan to shop the sales, take the time to think about what you really need —and what you plan to give. Americans spent $10 billion dollars on unwanted gifts in 2024. And last year, 65% of consumers reported returning a holiday gift, while 54% admitted to regifting an unwanted item. So, being more intentional about your holiday shopping can benefit both your wallet and the planet. “We are in an era right now where things are very expensive , and so when we're talking about affordability and Black Friday, thinking about what's really going to serve us and make us happy is a great way of thinking about sustainability too,” says Shelie Miller co-director of the Center for Sustainable Systems at the University of Michigan. “Being thoughtful about what's happening to our bank accounts as well as the overall amount of stuff we're buying can be very helpful as far as guiding us to a better path forward.” We spoke with experts about how best to avoid overconsumption and shop with sustainability in mind this Black Friday. Plan your shopping—and stick to the list Before you shop, create a list of what you’re looking for to avoid any unwanted impulse purchases. “Having a list and sticking to it can be helpful for curbing some of those impulsive consumptions when that impulsivity is sky high,” says Karen Winterich, professor of marketing at Penn State University. When you’re shopping, think twice before jumping on any deals for items that weren’t on your list. “We often get sucked into buying because it feels like a good deal,” says Winterich. “It makes us feel good to get that deal, and then later we may actually feel regret. Like, ‘I got a good deal, but did I even need to buy in the first place?’” To avoid feeling any regret, focus on how much you’re spending rather than how much you’re saving. “Even if we're saving a lot, we're still spending,” says Winterich. “If it's 90% off, but I don't need it, I'm not going to use it. Don't buy it.” Be intentional with your gifts If you’re buying gifts for the holiday season, take some time to think about the person you’re shopping for before you swipe your card. “If you're buying for someone else, pause and think about the person and if [the gift] is something they would really want and enjoy and use, or if you’re buying it to check the box, and say, ‘I got them a gift,’” says Winterich. If you know your friend has a cupboard full of coffee mugs, consider getting them locally roasted coffee beans or treating them to a coffee instead of buying them another mug. Consider gifting something people can consume—especially if you’re buying for someone you don’t know very well, like an office Secret Santa or a new neighbor. “Maybe that’s a loaf of local bread or something you make yourself with a locally made jam, or it could be some hot chocolate mix with a special treat attached to it,” says Winterich. “Something that's consumable and not necessarily made from plastics and shipped overseas, but a little bit more locally made, that they're going to consume and not have sitting around or donating. [It conveys] ‘I'm still thinking of you, I'm still giving you a gift, but it's not stuff that is going to sit there that you’re not going to enjoy and appreciate.” Consider your footprint Individual actions may not seem like much, but their impact can add up. Every year, people in the United States throw out more than 34 billion lbs of used textiles— roughly 100 lbs of textile waste per person each year—while global electronic waste continues to climb . If you’re buying an item online, see if you can pick it up at the store. Last mile delivery, the final step before a product reaches your doorstop, is responsible for roughly half of a delivery’s total emissions. “If you know you're already going to be going to the store, maybe you could just pick out one day in the week and say I'm going to hit these couple stores up where I have items to pick up at, rather than having that individual last mile delivery,” says Winterich. Consider shopping for quality rather than quantity—and be mindful of what you might already have at home. “A lot of times with impulse buys we're trying to get as much stuff for as little money as possible,” says Miller. “When we're talking about sustainability, we want people to use items for a long time to get their best environmental value.” “Everything that we buy had [manufacturing and shipping] impacts that were many times bigger than the product itself,” continues Miller. “So [thinking] maybe that stocking stuffer isn't really going to bring joy, and it's just going to affect my pocketbook. That actually has some environmental [benefits] to it.”

items.originalTitle: Why You Should Train to Be Ethically Fit
items.author: David W. Miller and Susan Richardson
items.title: Why You Should Train to Be Ethically Fit
items.summary: —oxygen—Getty Images Think of great athletes; they are fit in a way that relies on years of training and practice. An accomplished track star did not suddenly decide to run the four-minute mile one morning and have all the skills, strength, and endurance to do it. Elite tennis players prepare for and anticipate mid-game scenarios and know just what shot to draw on because they’ve practiced it thousands of times. Or think of great musicians who are fit because they’ve practiced scales, arpeggios, and studies for years before they perform a challenging work. A brilliant cellist did not suddenly decide to play the Bach cello suites one morning and have it artfully under her fingers immediately. They have cultivated their ability by keeping the skills going all along. In each case, they developed and practiced their skills—their fitness or wellness, so to speak—over time so they would be ready when they’re playing in pressure-packed moments under the bright lights. Our research and experience convince us that we can become and stay ethically fit by cultivating ethical strength and agility so that, when the moment comes, the muscle patterns and range of motion we need are there. The question for many then becomes how to get those muscles and then keep them in shape. You could certainly delve into the great classical schools of ethics, reading in-depth tomes by thinkers past and present. You could probe the great ancient spiritual and religious traditions for their wisdom on the human struggle with right and wrong and the practices that can help. You could read policies and laws related to ethics, which would easily take up multiple volumes (and lots of time). Or you might look to recent psychological and neurological studies on the way our brains work and why, realizing the “right” thing may be trickier than we think. These are all great things to do… if you have the time and the bandwidth. But for many of us, life’s demands mean that instead, we need to harvest the core ideas from all these traditions and craft an intellectually robust, informed, and practical set of ethical tools while also cultivating the strength to wield them. You can move from simply having knowledge—the ethical exercises—to having wisdom, a reflective way of looking at decisions in your life and indeed at yourself. I hope that as you think about what success looks like in your life, and what you want it to look like in the future, such wisdom will be part of it. Life is all about decisions, in which we act out—and often find out—who we are. There are a range of ways to think about how ethics works in our lives. But given how decisions both draw on who we’ve been and shape who we’re becoming, we’ll focus here on decision-making as an elevated moment in the ethical landscape of our lives. How we want to see ourselves as behaving and how we actually behave in the moment, or our “lived ethic,” can all too easily be two different things. As you reflect honestly on your recent decisions, what is your own lived ethic? What is mine? And how can it be wiser and more informed for the sake of your future self and those you care about? Experiences from the past, things in the moment that can throw us off balance, and an unrealistic sense of the future can make a sound ethical decision difficult to discern. What we need are the tools and practices for effectively tackling ethical decisions, particularly when the dilemma is in the ethical gray zone or, worse, disguised and unrecognizable until it is too late. Ethics is not simply about laws and compliance. Rather, it’s also about character (yours) and culture (your organization’s). This is not to take away from compliance officers and departments; indeed, hopefully, it will affirm their importance as one place in the larger picture. Compliance departments and guidelines are necessary but not sufficient. They tend to look backward, focused on catching those who’ve violated laws and regulations, whereas ethics understood as character and culture is focused on avoiding future mistakes. Law, codes, and policy are an important place to begin, but we need to use other ethical perspectives as well. Similarly, ethics is not merely about telling people to be “good” or “moral,” an approach that can be misleading and unhelpful. First, telling someone just to “be moral” can put inordinate pressure on them without giving them the tools they need to fulfill the expectation. And telling people to be good can also be interpreted in too many ways. More helpful is an approach that helps you identify ethical problems as such and know your own ethical sources and tools for making an ethical decision. Such an approach helps you better imagine possible outcomes, either positive or negative, and see yourself working through them. But if ethics isn’t only about compliance or the admonition to be good, then what else is it? My view is that it also gathers the two critical pieces of character and culture, which in turn invite deeper questions. What shapes and sustains your individual character or the corporate culture of the business or organization you’re a part of? What role (if any) do religious or spiritual traditions play in either one? For many, their faith tradition—even if they move away from the doctrinal claims or practices—remains influential, if not central, to their ethical grounding and sense of societal responsibility. What other sources or reality checks do you use in ethical decision-making—a mentor, for instance, or a close family member you check in with? How carefully do you track and trust your intuition and gut instinct? Your lived ethic is the behavior and values you personally bring into an ethical decision. But the fact is you’re never there alone. You are in an ethical field, which can be compared with a playing field in sports. That field comprises the context in which your personal ethics and decision-making is taking place, including external factors, organizational ethics, and the ethics of other people. For ethical decisions, we are rarely solo actors. Excerpted from T he 5 Questions for Ethical Decisions: How to Succeed Without Selling Your Soul by David W. It’s certainly ambitious – but will they be able to fill it? ‘A cathedral of cars” is how the colossal Citroën garage in Brussels was described when it opened in 1934, conceived as a startling glass temple to showcase the streamlined wonders of the automobile age. It greeted the street with an immense curtain wall of glass that wrapped a monumental nave-like showroom, culminating in a curved art deco prow, which glowed like a crystal lantern by night. Consequently, after a €230m decade-long transformation in collaboration with the Pompidou Centre, this gargantuan garage has been reborn as a palace of performance, dance, music, film, architecture and visual art. items.originalTitle: How the Gaza Encampments Unleashed the Blue Tsunami and Helped Spark a Worldwide Movement
items.author: Safia Southey
items.title: How the Gaza Encampments Unleashed the Blue Tsunami and Helped Spark a Worldwide Movement
items.summary: Contagion is real. Measles has come roaring back in the U.S. because of the rise of public health skeptics and reckless government officials — chief among them Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. — who have undermined faith in humanity’s best defense against the once-eliminated, vaccine-preventable viral disease. But there is another type of contagion out there, a beneficial variant, also fanned by the policies of foolish government officials: political protest. When America looks back to the high-water marks of modern activism, “the Sixties” comes to mind: the civil rights movement, the anti-Vietnam War movement, women’s liberation, LGBTQ+ liberation, and a plethora of other rights movements. In each case, young people were the shock troops of change, the activists leading the way. But “the Sixties” weren’t confined to the United States. In Vietnam, the war against the U.S. invaders was fought, in large measure, by young people. The same year that U.S. troops there were rocked by the Vietnamese forces’ Tet Offensive — 1968 — France erupted in student occupations, and Mexico saw a student uprising that led to a massacre by government forces. During that era, from student protests in Japan to youth at the forefront of Czechoslovakia’s Prague Spring, young people across the world were in revolt. New research shows this protest contagion is real — and has continued. A recently published study of 15 years of protests across 30 European countries found “robust evidence” that “protest activity in one year significantly increases protest frequency in the following year, and protests in one country contribute to the onset of protests in neighboring states.” All it takes is a spark somewhere and a realization that what one person can do, another can do: Stand up, speak out, sit in, march on. Today, Safia Southey examines how the righteous rage of the 2024 Gaza solidarity campus encampments — which she was a part of — became the catalyst of the blue tsunami that swept across America earlier this month and may be in the process of circling the globe, from Serbia to India. Establishment types want to take credit for the election just past. Southey sets the record straight on who won and why, as well as where the movement goes from here. —Nick Turse, editor of TomDispatch If you haven’t yet, sign up to receive TomDispatch in your inbox here. The Hidden Backstory of the Blue Wave Students at Columbia University set up tents on the lawn at the center of campus in April 2024 and said they would stay until the university divested from Israel’s war on Gaza. Within weeks, encampments had spread to campuses across the country , and soon around the world . I was a law student at Columbia that spring and spent much of it in the encampment. I remember the cold nights and the teach-ins on the grass, the food that kept arriving from strangers, a Passover seder held on the lawn, and students praying in rows beside the tents. Young people were told that their objection was a luxury the country could not afford. Those who watched from a distance may remember a different set of images: riot police dragging students across their own campuses , an Emory economics professor thrown to the ground by officers, and a spring in which more than 2,000 people were arrested at protests nationwide. By the summer, the tents were gone. The bombing of Gaza continued. In the 2024 presidential race, these same young people who had spent the spring organizing were asked to support a ticket that would not break with the policy they had protested. They were told that their objection was a luxury the country could not afford. Months before the encampments, more than 100,000 Michigan Democrats had voted “uncommitted” to warn the party about Israel’s onslaught, but the warning went largely unheeded. Many of us voted that November with dread, and some could not bring themselves to vote at all. Related How Columbia’s Leadership Refashioned the University in Trump’s Image Donald Trump won the presidency, and within only a few months, federal immigration agents had detained Mahmoud Khalil (who had negotiated on the encampment’s behalf), and Columbia had agreed to pay more than $200 million to the administration that was punishing its students. By then, much of the commentary class had decided the protests had alienated voters and might even have helped elect Trump. The midterm election results told a very different story. Darializa Avila Chevalier, who was arrested alongside students at Columbia’s encampment in 2024, won the congressional seat that includes the university , after unseating a five-term incumbent in June’s primary. In Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed , who ran openly against his own party’s position on Gaza, won a seat in the Senate. Democrats took back both the House and the Senate, and they did it by winning in places the party had stopped imagining it could compete: Texas, South Carolina, Kansas, to name a few, while also flipping Senate seats in Ohio and Maine. When Zohran Mamdani was elected mayor of New York City a year ago, plenty of commentators treated it as a local story , one that could only happen there ; the midterm results show they were wrong. This election was enormous, and the encampments belong at the center of the story of how it happened. Gaza was the source of the anger: For two years, a generation watched the genocide on their phones in real time, while the people they had been raised to trust explained why nothing could be done . The encampments and the wider student movement gave that anger somewhere to go, taught people how to organize, and even more importantly, showed them the institutions meant to protect them simply would not . If young people wanted to be represented, we realized we would have to build that representation ourselves. Learning From the Encampments Many of the students who joined the encampments had never organized anything before. Within days — especially after the original organizers were arrested — they were running a small town: rotating security shifts, feeding hundreds of people, coordinating legal observers and jail support , holding meetings late into the night to decide by consensus what to do next, and negotiating with administrators who had far more power than they did. Students learned how to bring a demand to an institution, how to build a coalition across groups that did not always agree, and how to keep people together after arrests and suspensions. Jewish, Muslim, Arab, Black, and Latino students, graduate workers, faculty, and neighbors from Harlem and Morningside Heights in New York City learned to work beside one another. Political campaigns run on those same skills, and plenty of people who staffed jail-support lines in 2024 were staffing phone banks two years later. Related “A New Sense of World-Building”: Inside the Student Movement for Gaza Socialist organizers were part of that education from the start. Members of the Young Democratic Socialists of America helped set up encampments from the University of California, Berkeley to New York City’s Hunter College, and the culture there — with mass meetings, shared labor, and decisions made together — already resembled the organizing that the Democratic Socialists of America had been practicing in tenant unions and on picket lines for years. The students also learned what their universities would do when tested. Columbia presented itself as a place for open debate and then called the police on its own students, suspended and expelled them, and later settled with the federal government to restore its funding while one of the encampment’s negotiators sat in immigration detention. Students who had been taught that their schools existed to protect free inquiry watched those schools choose their endowments and their relationships with power instead. Many of them had already watched law firms withdraw job offers from students who had signed statements about Gaza in the fall of 2023. The lesson was harsh and clarifying: No institution was coming to save them. The Democratic Party gave them no reason to think otherwise. Even after Biden withdrew and Kamala Harris became the nominee, the policy stayed where it was, and at the party’s convention that August, organizers rejected the Uncommitted delegates’ request to have a Palestinian American speak on the main stage. For a generation already disillusioned with their universities, this confirmed that if Gen Z wanted their voices heard in the halls of power, they would need to knock on the doors, recruit the candidates, raise the money through small donations, and build the organizations themselves. From the Lawn to the Ballot Mamdani’s mayoral campaign was the first clear sign that they had started that work. He grew out of that energy, and his campaign gave it a direction. His primary victory in June 2025 rested on years of organizing by tenants, socialists, workers, and Palestine solidarity groups, and much of it ran through New York City DSA, whose electoral organizers described the coalition behind him as young New Yorkers becoming politically active, tenants, and voters drawn to both his affordability agenda and his support for Palestinian rights . Sociologist Heba Gowayed traced the protest movement’s contribution to his win within days of the result. More than 50,000 people signed up to volunteer during that primary. Many of them were young people who had never knocked on a door for a candidate before, and they learned to canvass the way they had learned to run an encampment: quickly, from one another, and because no one else was going to do it for them. A campaign that talked about both affordability and Palestinian rights gave them a reason to give up their evenings and weekends. When he won the general election, more than 2 million New Yorkers had voted , the most in a mayoral race since 1969. Related There’s a New Democratic Machine. It’s Unabashedly Socialist. Mamdani’s victory changed what seemed possible for everyone watching. Candidates who had been warned that criticizing Israel would end their careers could now point to New York. Reps. Rashida Tlaib and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, currently the only members of DSA in Congress, will be joined by a record number of DSA-endorsed candidates, at least six. Claire Valdez, a state assembly member who had joined protests calling for an arms embargo on Israel, won the open seat in New York’s 7th Congressional District. In Colorado, Melat Kiros, a 29-year-old lawyer who lost her job after refusing to take down a social media post criticizing law firms over their positions on Israel and Palestine, unseated Rep. Diana DeGette, who had held the seat for three decades. Avila Chevalier remains the clearest line from the lawn to the Capitol. She is a Columbia alumna who stood with students through arrests and threats of expulsion, and who had spent years in immigrant rights and community organizing before that spring. She ran with the backing of the same democratic socialists who had helped elect Mamdani. After her primary, Maryam Alwan, who protested at Columbia in 2024 (and with whom I am proud to have studied at Sciences Po Menton in France), told Al Jazeera what it meant to see “Darializa, a former leader and organiser of the encampment, represent the school that arrested her.” Gowayed, the sociologist, put the connection more bluntly: “This does not happen if those students don’t encamp; it just doesn’t happen.” “This Is an Uprising,” by Mark and Paul Engler. Available on Bookshop.org . In Michigan, the state where the uncommitted vote first registered the party’s Gaza problem, Seed the Vote organized Jewish, Muslim, and Arab volunteers to knock doors for El-Sayed together, alongside IfNotNow and Bend the Arc. El-Sayed spoke directly to voters’ anger over the party’s position on Gaza and asked them to elect someone who shared it. For anyone who had been in the encampments, those canvasses would have looked familiar. Khalil, who was released from detention in June 2025 and is still facing deportation , pointed to El-Sayed and Mamdani a week before the election as evidence that politics was shifting. “The American public is finally changing, is finally looking at the Palestinian as an equal human,” he said . Anger at Trump, the cost of living, and organizations with decades of history all helped produce the blue tsunami, and no election return can isolate the share owed to the encampments. For people who had already concluded that their leaders were willing to fund devastation in Gaza while claiming there was no money for housing or healthcare at home, the war with Iran confirmed the judgment. By October, polls compiled by Responsible Statecraft found voters were more worried about the war than about immigration or crime, and 6 in 10 opposed U.S. military action against Iran. The candidates who won on Election Day week treated rent, healthcare, and war as one argument about whose lives the government is willing to sacrifice, and young voters answered them. Lessons for Serbia and India Americans were not the only ones to see a student movement reach the ballot this fall. In November 2024, the canopy of the Novi Sad railway station collapsed and killed 16 people, and Serbian students, blaming the corruption they believed had made the disaster possible, blockaded their faculties and demanded accountability. Inside the blockades, they ran themselves through plenums and open assemblies with no leaders; every decision went to a vote. In March 2025, they invited the rest of the country to do the same, and within 10 days, citizens had formed their own assemblies , called zborovi , in neighborhoods and towns from Niš to Novi Sad. That same month, roughly 300,000 people filled Belgrade for the largest protest in Serbia’s history, but a moment of silence for the victims ended in panic when the crowd scattered from what protesters and analysts said was a sonic weapon ; the government denied using one. Related Mahmoud Khalil: “We Can’t Afford to Stay Silent” In May 2025, the students began calling for snap parliamentary elections . Serbian opposition politics had long concentrated on the cities and left smaller towns and villages to the ruling party, so the students went there, knocking on doors in places where the state media had branded them terrorists. On October 25, almost two years after the collapse, the Students’ List group won 140 of Parliament’s 250 seats and ended Aleksandar Vučić’s party’s hold on government. The plenums had taught them how to make decisions together, keep thousands of people moving in the same direction, and earn trust one conversation at a time — skills they carried over into election campaigning. Few people would have predicted that outcome during the first winter of the blockades, when the students were being dismissed as naïve. In India, young people organized under the banner of the Cockroach Janta Party have been in the streets since September, together with student groups and opposition parties, protesting a revision of the voter rolls that has removed more than 130 million names. Police have detained thousands of them, and it would be easy to judge that movement by what it wins this month. Two years from now, we may have a better sense of what it set in motion. Read Our Complete Coverage TomDispatch What Comes Next Nothing that happened on Election Day can repair what was done to Gaza, and the encampments’ original demands remain unmet. The students were protesting the killing of Palestinians and their own institutions’ complicity in it, and electing a former organizer to Congress will not change American policy toward Israel on its own. The organizations that carried these candidates into office will need to stay independent enough to press them once they arrive, and the voters who returned to the Democratic Party this year came back on conditions. Officials who forget this should expect the same organizers to come for their seats. For those of us who felt crushed in 2024, though, the midterm victories deserve to be fully absorbed and celebrated. We were told that the protests had failed, that we had cost the party an election, that our anger was a liability. The people who had every reason to give up kept meeting instead. They recruited friends, built campaigns, found candidates they could believe in , and spent two years knocking on doors in neighborhoods where no one expected them. While the news cycle may measure movements in weeks, it wrote this one off before most of its participants had graduated. The verdict came on Election Day, two years late, and it was written by the same people who had been dismissed. We did it, or at least we started to. The work ahead is harder, and it will take longer than anyone would like, but it starts now, with the wind at our backs. items.author: Sarah Wynn-Williams
items.title: Careless People author Sarah Wynn-Williams: ‘The silence is mine, it doesn’t have to be yours’
items.summary: Since writing her bestselling exposé, the former employee has been forbidden from speaking publicly about Meta. In an exclusive extract from her Orwell lecture, she describes life under a gag order – and why it’s time to speak out against big tech In 2011, Sarah Wynn-Williams was appointed director of global public policy at Facebook (now Meta). Over seven years, she brokered meetings with world leaders and contributed to public policy strategy in developing nations across three continents . She left the company in 2017 and in March 2025 published a book about her time at Meta. Careless People: A Story of Where I Used to Work describes a journey of disillusionment with a company that she was sure would change the world for the better to one “helping some of the worst people in the world do terrible things ”. It contains allegations of a toxic internal culture, including sexual harassment and gender-based discriminatory practices.

items.originalTitle: Stormy Thanksgiving weather causes delays and damages for many Americans
items.author: Lisa Desjardins
items.title: Stormy Thanksgiving weather causes delays and damages for many Americans
items.summary: A stormy Thanksgiving day led to serious flooding, major power outages and disrupted travel plans. By Thursday evening, more than 900,000 customers were without power in at least eight states. The East Coast is grappling with a pair of storm systems affecting people from Maine to Florida. This as strong winds battered the West Coast from Oregon to California. Lisa Desjardins reports.
